Let me start with a quick aside: When people talk about rising costs of college tuition, I am usually quick to point out that it's the result of a distorted supply-demand relationship. Student loans are very easy to come by these days. Looking at the problem simply: Let's say I want to sell someone a table I had built and planned to charge them $200. If I learn that that same person has access to a $300 loan with very little paperwork that they won't have to pay off or even really think about for a few years, it's only natural for me to raise my table's cost to $500. So of course, tuition has only gone up as the students themselves don't really feel the pinch - and besides, they need a degree, right?

Reflecting on the social changes of the last century, the trends all tend to have an end result of serving to make citizens as a whole less independent, less stable and more isolated. To anyone who has been paying attention at all, this is obviously no surprise. However, a particularly devious element just dawned on me today: encouraging women to see the workplace as their first option has to be very close to the top of the list of societal fuck-ups.

I feel like it took years of conditioning breaking to even consider this possibility, but as someone who's hoping to eventually own a home and some land, the pieces just came together.

It used to be that a father would work to support his wife and children for the most part. That means a single income family, as opposed to a double income family. So when a contractor goes to build a house, it is built in such a way that it can ultimately be sold to someone. Knowing that a single income family is the most common buyer, homes are built in a price range that meets their buying capacity for the most part.

Enter feminism. Women are sold on the idea of empowerment and equality. And guess what? The average total family income doubles. And just like with the student loan problem, homes start being built for families who have two incomes - i.e. twice as expensive.

Basically, if you're ever frustrated about high housing costs: thank a feminist.
